subject: Archaeology
subcategory: Lost Cities of the Ancient World
title: Teotihuacan: City of the Gods
description: A micro-lesson that makes Teotihuacan: City of the Gods usable.

hook.text: The largest city in the ancient Americas had 100,000 residents. Nobody knows what its builders called themselves.

buildup.text: Teotihuacan's Pyramid of the Sun is the third-largest pyramid on Earth, built around 100 CE near modern Mexico City.

discovery.text: The city was planned on a grid with a two-mile central avenue. It had apartment complexes and a sewer system.

twist.text: Around 550 CE, the city was deliberately burned from the inside. Evidence suggests an internal revolt, not invasion.

climax.text: A robot exploring a tunnel under the Pyramid found liquid mercury and thousands of golden orbs in 2014.

punchline.text: A nameless people built an empire and burned it down themselves.

quiz.question: What evidence suggests Teotihuacan was destroyed from within?
options: Foreign weapons were found in the ruins
The city was burned from the inside, pointing to an internal revolt
Written records describe a civil war between priests and warriors

details.summary: Teotihuacan, near modern Mexico City, was the largest city in the Americas at its peak around 450 CE, home to over 100,000 people. Its massive Pyramid of the Sun and Moon, wide Avenue of the Dead, and apartment compounds reveal a sophisticated urban society whose builders remain anonymous.
details.whyItMatters: Teotihuacan was a metropolis that influenced all Mesoamerican civilizations for centuries, yet we do not know what its people called themselves or their city.
takeaways: The largest city in the Americas, with over 100,000 residents by 450 CE
The builders' identity and language remain completely unknown
It influenced Mesoamerican civilizations for centuries after its fall

faq.question: Why don't we know who built Teotihuacan?
faq.answer: No decipherable writing system has been found there. The Aztecs, who discovered it already in ruins, named it Teotihuacan — City of the Gods — believing only deities could have built it. The builders' ethnic identity, language, and political system remain subjects of scholarly debate.

faq.question: What caused Teotihuacan's collapse?
faq.answer: Around 550 CE, the city's ceremonial center was deliberately burned — likely by its own inhabitants during an internal revolt. Resource depletion, political tensions, and competition from rival cities may have triggered the upheaval.
